Evidence check. Errors: 0 5xx on both sides, every endpoint, every window — no availability regression. Central latency: canary matches or beats stable on p50 (33 vs 35 overall; 22/47/79 vs 22/47/82 per endpoint) and ties on p95 (95 vs 95 overall; 27/60/102 vs 27/59/103). Stability over time: canary p95 is 95/95/92/95 across the four 30s windows vs stable 96/93/94/97 — flat, no drift or warmup trend, no late-window blowup.

The only anomaly is tail-only and endpoint-local: canary /search p99 = 652ms vs stable 61ms, which also explains the canary overall p99 of 172 vs 104. Judgement on how to read it: (a) p50 and p95 on /search are identical (47/60 vs 47/59), so the distribution has not shifted — only a handful of extreme outliers moved; (b) with 729 canary /search requests, p99 is roughly the 7 slowest requests, so it is a statistically thin signal; (c) the comparison is structurally unfair at the tail — canary p99 comes from 1 pod while stable p99 is pooled across 3 pods, which dilutes any single pod's rare slow requests (GC pause, cold cache). A genuine code regression in search would be expected to move p50/p95 too, and it does not.

Risk weighing (judgement): worst case if the spike is real and persists at 100% traffic is ~1% of /search requests at ~650ms, still sub-second, with zero errors — degradation, not customer breakage. Blocking the release on a noisy single-pod p99 is the more likely error here. Decision: PROMOTE, with an explicit follow-up to watch /search p99 after the ramp. Next action: write the decision file.

{
  "decision": "PROMOTE",
  "why": "Health signals are clean and the one anomaly is a thin, tail-only artifact rather than a regression. EVIDENCE: (1) Zero 5xx on both sides - 0/2384 canary, 0/7404 stable, 0.00% err on every endpoint and in all four 30s windows. (2) Canary matches or beats stable on central latency: overall p50 33ms vs 35ms, overall p95 95ms vs 95ms; per endpoint p50/p95 are /browse 22/27 vs 22/27, /search 47/60 vs 47/59, /checkout 79/102 vs 82/103. (3) No drift over time: canary p95 is 95, 95, 92, 95 across the four windows vs stable 96, 93, 94, 97 - flat, no warmup ramp and no late-window blowup. (4) The sole outlier is canary /search p99 652ms vs stable 61ms, which also accounts for the canary overall p99 of 172ms vs 104ms.

JUDGEMENT on that p99 spike: it is most likely outlier noise, not a code regression. First, /search p50 (47ms) and p95 (60ms) are identical to stable, so the latency distribution has not shifted - only a few extreme samples moved; a real regression in the search path would be expected to push p50 or p95 as well. Second, the signal is statistically thin: with 729 canary /search requests, p99 is set by roughly the 7 slowest requests. Third, the comparison is structurally unfair at the tail - canary p99 comes from a single pod, while stable p99 is pooled across 3 pods, which dilutes any individual pod's rare slow requests (GC pause, cold cache, one-off stall).

JUDGEMENT on risk: if the spike were real and persisted at 100% traffic, the blast radius is about 1% of /search requests at roughly 650ms - still sub-second, with zero errors or timeouts. That is mild degradation, not customer breakage, so the cost of a false rollback (blocking the release on single-pod p99 noise) outweighs it.

FOLLOW-UP: this promote is conditional on monitoring. During and after the ramp to 100%, watch /search p99 and max latency specifically; if p99 stays elevated with a larger sample, or p95 starts to move, roll back. Re-measuring /search tail latency with more canary pods or a longer run would have removed the single-pod sampling ambiguity before this call."
